title: ☕ JAVA & SPRING
meta: This is a trigger file, not study material. Question visible → answer OUT LOUD → then expand → grade what you missed.
Bullets are keywords and flows, not explanations. If you need the explanation, you're in the wrong file — go to the note.
⭐ = decides the round. 🔥 = trending 2026. 📍 = you were asked this. 🏢 = reported asked in a named real loop (not yours — see [[TREND-SCAN-2026-08]]). 📝 = no vault note yet.

questions.text: 🏢 "How does HashMap work internally, and what happens when two keys collide?
points: Array of buckets; index from hash(key) spread (XOR high bits) to reduce clustering
Collision → linked list in the bucket → red-black tree at threshold 8 (and ≥64 buckets)
Resize at load factor 0.75 → capacity doubles → entries rehashed
Treeification is a defence against hash-collision DoS, not a normal path
Not thread-safe; concurrent resize historically caused infinite loops
questions.flow: hash → spread → bucket → list → tree at 8 → resize at 0.75
questions.trap: stopping at "it's a hash table with linked lists" — the treeify threshold is the follow-up

questions.text: 🏢 "What happens if you use a mutable object as a HashMap key?
points: Hash is computed at insert; mutating the key changes the hash afterwards
Entry is now in the wrong bucket → get misses, containsKey false, entry unreachable
Effectively a memory leak — it can't be found or removed
Hence: keys should be immutable, or at least never mutated while in a map
Same reason equals/hashCode must be consistent and use the same fields
questions.flow: hash captured at insert → mutation moves the true hash → lookup probes wrong bucket → stranded entry
questions.trap: saying "it just won't be found" without naming the leak

questions.text: 🏢 "Fail-fast vs fail-safe iterators.
points: Fail-fast (ArrayList, HashMap) — modCount checked; structural change → ConcurrentModificationException
It's best-effort, not a guarantee — never build logic on catching CME
Fail-safe (CopyOnWriteArrayList, ConcurrentHashMap) — iterate a snapshot or weakly-consistent view
Cost: COW copies the whole array per write; CHM iterator may miss concurrent updates
Single-threaded CME is usually list.remove() inside a for-each → use Iterator.remove or removeIf

links.label: Fail Fast vs Fail Safe Iteration

questions.flow: modCount → CME (best effort) · snapshot/weakly-consistent → no CME but stale
questions.trap: calling fail-safe "thread-safe iteration with full consistency"

questions.text: 🏢 "What is a Spring bean, and what is the container actually doing?
points: Bean = object whose lifecycle the container owns — creation, wiring, destruction
IoC: you declare dependencies, the container resolves and supplies them
Definitions from component scan / @Bean methods / imports → BeanDefinition registry
Constructor injection is the default recommendation — immutable, testable, fails fast on cycles
Not magic: it's a registry, a graph resolve, and often a proxy on top
questions.flow: definitions registered → graph resolved → instantiate → inject → post-process → ready
questions.trap: "a bean is any object" — ownership of the lifecycle is the distinction

questions.text: Bean scopes — and the trap in the common one.
points: singleton (default, one per container) · prototype (new each request) · web: request, session, application
The trap: a singleton injecting a prototype gets it once — it never gets a fresh one
Fixes: ObjectProvider / @Lookup / scoped proxy
Singleton beans must be stateless, or you've built a shared-mutable-state bug
Scoped proxies are how a request-scoped bean survives injection into a singleton
questions.flow: singleton default → prototype injected once → use provider or scoped proxy
questions.trap: expecting a prototype to refresh per call inside a singleton

questions.text: 🏢 "A class implements two interfaces with the same default method. What happens?
points: Compile error — ambiguous, the compiler will not choose for you
Resolve explicitly: override and call InterfaceName.super.method()
Rules: class wins over interface; more specific sub-interface wins over super-interface
Default methods exist for interface evolution without breaking implementors — not for multiple inheritance of state
Still no state: interfaces have no instance fields, so the diamond problem stays limited
questions.flow: ambiguous → compile error → override → X.super.method() · class beats interface
questions.trap: guessing a resolution order instead of naming the compile error

questions.text: Walk me through the bean lifecycle.
points: Definition → instantiate → populate (inject) → Aware callbacks
BeanPostProcessor.before → @PostConstruct / afterPropertiesSet / init-method → .after
The after step is where proxies are created — AOP, @Transactional, @Async all land here
Destruction: @PreDestroy / DisposableBean — singletons only, prototypes aren't tracked
BeanFactoryPostProcessor acts earlier, on definitions, before any instantiation
questions.flow: instantiate → inject → aware → BPP.before → init → BPP.after = proxy → ready → destroy
questions.trap: not knowing proxying happens post-init — it explains every self-invocation bug

questions.text: 🏢 "You call a @Transactional method from another method of the same class. Does the transaction work?
points: No. Self-invocation goes through this, bypassing the proxy entirely — no advice runs
Same reason @Async, @Cacheable, @Retryable silently do nothing on internal calls
Fixes: split into another bean · self-inject · TransactionTemplate · AspectJ weaving
Also silent: @Transactional on a private/final method, or a non-public one
Rollback default is unchecked only — checked exceptions don't roll back unless declared
questions.flow: internal call → this, not proxy → no advice → move it to another bean
questions.trap: the checked-exception rollback default — the second half of this question

questions.text: JDK dynamic proxy or CGLIB — how does Spring choose?
points: Implements an interface → JDK dynamic proxy (interface-based) by default
No interface → CGLIB subclass; Boot defaults to CGLIB (proxyTargetClass=true)
CGLIB can't proxy final classes or final/private methods — advice silently absent
Proxy means a wrapper object: injected type is the proxy, not your instance
AspectJ weaving avoids proxies entirely, at build/load time — no self-invocation problem
questions.flow: interface → JDK · else → CGLIB subclass → final/private = no advice → AspectJ to escape
questions.trap: a final service class and hours lost to "why isn't it transactional"

questions.text: How does Boot auto-configuration actually decide?
points: @EnableAutoConfiguration → candidates from AutoConfiguration.imports (was spring.factories)
Each gated by @Conditional: OnClass, OnMissingBean, OnProperty, OnWebApplication
@ConditionalOnMissingBean is why your bean silently wins — back-off by design
Ordering via @AutoConfigureBefore/After; report available via --debug / actuator conditions
Classpath is the input, so a stray dependency changes behaviour
questions.flow: imports listed → conditions evaluated → back off if you defined it → debug report tells you why
questions.trap: calling it magic instead of naming @ConditionalOnMissingBean

questions.text: What does volatile guarantee, and what doesn't it?
points: Guarantees visibility + ordering (a write happens-before a subsequent read)
Does not give atomicity — count++ is read-modify-write, still racy
Prevents the reordering that breaks double-checked locking
Happens-before also established by: lock release/acquire, thread start/join, final-field publication
For atomic counters use AtomicLong / LongAdder, not volatile
questions.flow: visibility + ordering → but not atomic → compound ops still need CAS or a lock
questions.trap: volatile on a counter and calling it thread-safe

questions.text: How does ConcurrentHashMap get away without locking reads?
points: Reads are lock-free — nodes use volatile fields, so visibility is guaranteed
Writes lock a single bin (synchronized on the head node), not the whole map
Java 8 dropped segments; resize is cooperative — writers help transfer
size() is an estimate (CounterCells); iterators are weakly consistent
Compound ops need the atomic API: compute, merge, putIfAbsent — not get-then-put
questions.flow: volatile reads → per-bin write lock → cooperative resize → use atomic compound methods
questions.trap: if (!map.containsKey(k)) map.put(k,v) — still a race

questions.text: 🏢 "One API calls three services sequentially and it's slow. Fix it.
points: If independent → run in parallel: CompletableFuture.supplyAsync × 3 → allOf → join
Give it an explicit executor — the common ForkJoinPool is shared and small
thenCombine to merge, exceptionally/handle per branch for partial failure
Total latency becomes max(3), not sum(3) — say that number out loud
Per-call timeouts (orTimeout) or the slowest dependency defines your SLA
questions.flow: independent? → parallel futures on a dedicated pool → allOf → max not sum → per-call timeout
questions.trap: parallelising calls that are actually dependent, or using the common pool

questions.text: Trace a request through Spring MVC.
points: Filters (servlet, incl. security chain) → DispatcherServlet
HandlerMapping → handler + interceptor chain → HandlerAdapter invokes
Argument resolvers bind/validate params → your method → return value handlers
@ResponseBody → HttpMessageConverter (Jackson) → body
Exceptions → HandlerExceptionResolver → @ControllerAdvice / @ExceptionHandler
questions.flow: filters → dispatcher → mapping → adapter → resolvers → handler → converters → advice on error
questions.trap: placing @ControllerAdvice outside filters — it cannot catch a security-filter failure

questions.text: How does Spring Security actually intercept?
points: One servlet Filter (springSecurityFilterChain) delegating to an ordered chain
Authentication filter → AuthenticationManager → provider → SecurityContextHolder (ThreadLocal)
Authorisation at AuthorizationFilter; method security via proxies (so self-invocation applies again)
ThreadLocal context does not propagate to new threads — async/@Async needs explicit propagation
Stateless JWT: no session, verify signature + exp + aud, cache JWKS
questions.flow: filter chain → authenticate → context (ThreadLocal) → authorise → method security by proxy
questions.trap: losing the security context across an async boundary or a thread pool

questions.text: 🏢 "synchronized or ReentrantLock — where would you use the lock?
points: synchronized — JVM intrinsic, auto-release, biased/thin/fat escalation, simplest and usually right
ReentrantLock when you need what the keyword can't do: tryLock (with timeout), interruptible acquire, fairness, multiple Conditions
Cost: you own unlock() — must be in finally, or you leak the lock forever
ReadWriteLock / StampedLock for read-heavy shared state
Virtual threads changed the calculus — synchronized pinning was the reason to prefer locks; largely addressed in recent JDKs
questions.flow: default synchronized → need timeout/interrupt/fairness/conditions → ReentrantLock in try-finally
questions.trap: "ReentrantLock is faster" — under low contention they're comparable; it's about capability

questions.text: 🏢 "REQUIRED vs REQUIRES_NEW — and when does that bite?
points: REQUIRED (default) — join the caller's transaction, or start one; inner rollback marks the whole thing
REQUIRES_NEW — suspend the outer, run in a genuinely independent transaction, resume after
Classic use: audit/log rows that must survive a business rollback
Costs: two connections held at once — deadlock and pool-exhaustion risk under load
NESTED uses savepoints (JDBC only, not JPA-portable); MANDATORY/NEVER are assertions
questions.flow: join → REQUIRED · must survive outer rollback → REQUIRES_NEW → but two connections held
questions.trap: REQUIRES_NEW in a loop, exhausting the Hikari pool against itself

questions.text: Virtual threads or reactive?
points: Virtual threads: blocking code that scales — keep the imperative style, keep stack traces and debuggers
Reactive (WebFlux): backpressure as a first-class concept, streaming, composition operators
VT doesn't help CPU-bound work at all; it's a concurrency-count answer, not a throughput one
Migration reality: pinning on synchronized (largely resolved), thread-local heavy code, pooled resources still cap you
Honest 2026 answer: VT for most services, reactive where you genuinely need backpressure or streaming semantics
questions.flow: blocking + high concurrency → VT · backpressure/streaming → reactive · CPU-bound → neither
questions.trap: presenting VT as free throughput, or reactive as generally faster

questions.text: 🏢 "Two beans depend on each other. How does Spring handle it, and how do you fix it?
points: Constructor injection → fails at startup (BeanCurrentlyInCreationException) — it cannot be resolved
Field/setter injection can resolve via the early-reference cache — it "works", which is the trap
Boot 2.6+ disallows circular refs by default (allow-circular-references to opt back in)
Real fix is design: extract the shared concern into a third bean, or invert with an event
Escape hatches: @Lazy, ObjectProvider — treat as a smell, not a solution
questions.flow: constructor → hard fail · field → silently resolves → real fix is extracting the shared piece
questions.trap: reaching for @Lazy and calling it fixed

questions.text: When is a parallel stream the wrong call?
points: Uses the common ForkJoinPool — one shared pool for the whole JVM, sized to cores−1
One slow/blocking parallel stream starves every other user of that pool
Needs: large N, cheap splitting (array/ArrayList good, LinkedList bad), independent work, no shared mutable state
Boxing and small N usually make it slower than sequential
Blocking I/O in a parallel stream is the worst case — never do it
questions.flow: large N + splittable + CPU-bound + independent → maybe · blocking or shared state → no
questions.trap: .parallel() on a stream doing HTTP calls, poisoning the common pool

questions.text: 🏢 "Find duplicates in a list of integers with the Stream API.
points: groupingBy(identity(), counting()) → filter > 1 → keys
Or a Set + filter(n -> !seen.add(n)) — one pass, but stateful and unsafe in parallel
Say the trade-off: grouping is clear and parallel-safe, Set is O(n) with less allocation
distinct() needs correct equals/hashCode — ties back to #2
Mention ordering: groupingBy gives a HashMap — use LinkedHashMap if order matters
questions.flow: group by identity → count → filter >1 → keys · or seen-set single pass
questions.trap: the stateful-lambda version presented without noting it breaks under .parallel()

questions.text: Filter, interceptor, or AOP aspect?
points: Filter — servlet level, sees every request incl. unmatched; can wrap request/response bodies
Interceptor — Spring MVC level, knows the handler, preHandle/postHandle/afterCompletion
Aspect — any bean method, richest join points, but proxy-bound (self-invocation again)
Security and body/encoding concerns → filter · handler-aware cross-cutting → interceptor · service-layer concerns → aspect
Each extra layer costs stack depth and debuggability
questions.flow: protocol-level → filter · handler-aware → interceptor · method-level → aspect
questions.trap: an aspect for auth, then discovering it never fired on an internal call

questions.text: Checked or unchecked in a service layer?
points: Modern practice leans unchecked for the domain — checked exceptions leak through every signature
Checked is defensible where the caller genuinely can and must recover
Never catch (Exception e) and swallow; never throws Exception on a public API
Remember @Transactional rolls back on unchecked only by default (see #8) — this choice has transactional consequences
Design a domain hierarchy and map it to HTTP at the edge, not in the service
questions.flow: domain → unchecked hierarchy → mapped at the edge → rollback semantics follow
questions.trap: not connecting the checked/unchecked choice to rollback behaviour

questions.text: Constructor or field injection? Defend it.
points: Constructor: dependencies explicit, fields final, object always valid, trivially testable without Spring
Field injection hides dependencies, needs reflection to test, and hides cycles (see #19)
A constructor with eight args isn't a DI problem — it's the class telling you it does too much
Single constructor → @Autowired optional since 4.3
Setter injection for genuinely optional collaborators only
questions.flow: constructor → final + valid + testable → long arg list is a design signal, not a DI one
questions.trap: defending field injection with "it's less boilerplate" — Lombok already solved that

questions.text: Records — where do they fit?
points: Immutable, transparent data carriers: final fields, canonical constructor, equals/hashCode/toString generated
Perfect for DTOs, value objects, events, map keys (ties #2 — immutable key)
Compact constructor for validation/normalisation; can implement interfaces
Not for JPA entities — those need a no-arg constructor and mutability
With sealed types → exhaustive pattern matching, real algebraic modelling
questions.flow: immutable data carrier → DTO/event/value → compact constructor for invariants → sealed + switch
questions.trap: proposing records as JPA entities

questions.text: Spring, Quarkus or Micronaut — when would you not pick Spring?
points: Spring: runtime DI, reflection-heavy, unmatched ecosystem — the safe default
Micronaut/Quarkus: compile-time DI + AOT → fast startup, low memory, native-image friendly
That matters for serverless/Lambda, scale-to-zero, dense per-pod deployments
Spring Boot 3 + AOT/native closed much of the gap — the argument is weaker than in 2022
Real deciders: hiring pool, library support, team familiarity
questions.flow: startup/memory critical (serverless) → compile-time DI · else Spring · Boot AOT narrows it
questions.trap: framework benchmarks as the argument when hiring and ecosystem decide it

questions.text: Hibernate caching layers — which do you actually enable?
points: L1 = persistence context, per-session, always on, not optional
L2 = shared across sessions (Ehcache/Infinispan/Redis) — opt in per entity
Query cache needs L2 and is easy to get wrong; invalidation is the hard part
L2 shines on read-mostly reference data; it's a liability on hot mutable entities
In a clustered app, L2 needs a distributed/invalidating strategy or nodes diverge
questions.flow: L1 always → L2 for read-mostly reference data → query cache last and carefully
questions.trap: enabling L2 globally and creating stale-read bugs across nodes

questions.text: 🏢 "What's the N+1 problem in JPA and how do you solve it?
points: One query for the parents, then one per parent for a lazy association → N+1 round trips
Invisible in dev with 10 rows; catastrophic at 10,000
Fixes: JOIN FETCH · @EntityGraph · @BatchSize · projections/DTOs when you don't need entities
JOIN FETCH with pagination is a trap — Hibernate may paginate in memory
Detect it: SQL logging, hibernate.generate_statistics, an assertion on query count in tests
questions.flow: lazy association in a loop → N+1 → EntityGraph / JOIN FETCH / batch size → assert query count in tests
questions.trap: switching everything to EAGER — you've traded N+1 for loading the whole graph every time

questions.text: 🏢 "Memory climbs and the service dies with OOM every two days. Find it.
points: First: which OOM — heap, Metaspace, direct buffers, or native? The message tells you
Always-on -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError; analyse in MAT — dominator tree → GC roots
Usual suspects: unbounded cache/Map, ThreadLocal not cleared on a pooled thread, classloader leak on redeploy, listeners never unregistered
Confirm with GC logs: live-set after full GC trending up = real leak, not just pressure
Live triage: jcmd GC.heap_info, jmap -histo:live, JFR
questions.flow: identify the OOM kind → heap dump → dominator tree → find the GC root holding it
questions.trap: raising -Xmx and calling it fixed — that buys days, not a diagnosis

questions.text: Which collector, and what would you actually tune?
points: G1 default — region-based, pause-target driven, good general throughput/latency balance
ZGC / Shenandoah — concurrent, sub-millisecond pauses at large heaps, some throughput cost
Serial/Parallel still right for small containers or batch throughput jobs
Tune heap size and pause target first; resist per-flag micro-tuning without GC logs
Allocation rate is usually the real lever — fewer garbage objects beats a cleverer collector
questions.flow: measure allocation + pauses → G1 default → ZGC for large-heap latency → tune size/target, not flags
questions.trap: copying GC flags from a blog post with no GC log to justify them

questions.text: How big should the connection pool be?
points: Small. Pool size is bounded by database cores/disks, not by your thread count
Real DB load = pool × instances — the pod count is the multiplier people forget
Hikari: maximumPoolSize, connectionTimeout (fail fast), leakDetectionThreshold
Symptom of undersizing or of leaks looks identical: connection-timeout errors under load
Never hold a connection across a remote call — especially not across an LLM call
questions.flow: size to DB capacity → multiply by pods → fail-fast timeout → narrow the hold time
questions.trap: growing the pool to fix latency caused by long-held transactions

questions.text: LazyInitializationException in the controller. Why, and what's the right fix?
points: Session/persistence context closed at the transaction boundary; lazy proxy touched after → boom
Wrong fixes: EAGER everywhere · open-session-in-view (default-on in Boot, and it hides N+1 in the view layer)
Right fix: fetch what you need inside the transaction — @EntityGraph, JOIN FETCH, or a DTO projection
Cleanest: never let entities cross the service boundary; map to DTOs
Turn OSIV off deliberately so this fails loudly in dev, not silently in prod
questions.flow: context closed → lazy touched later → fetch inside the boundary → return DTOs → disable OSIV
questions.trap: leaving OSIV on and shipping a view layer quietly issuing queries

questions.text: Size a thread pool, and say what happens when it's full.
points: CPU-bound ≈ cores · I/O-bound ≈ cores × (1 + wait/service) — measure, don't guess
Bounded queue always; an unbounded queue converts overload into OOM and hides it
Rejection policy is a design decision: AbortPolicy (fail fast) · CallerRuns (natural backpressure) · discard (data loss)
Separate pools per dependency — a bulkhead, so one slow upstream can't consume everything
Name your threads, or the stack dump during an incident tells you nothing
questions.flow: measure wait/service → size → bounded queue → explicit rejection → bulkhead per dependency
questions.trap: Executors.newCachedThreadPool() in production — unbounded thread creation

questions.text: 🏢 "One request crosses five services. How do you trace it end to end?
points: W3C traceparent propagated on every hop — HTTP headers and message headers alike
Micrometer Tracing / OpenTelemetry auto-instruments the common clients; MDC puts trace ID in logs
Async and messaging break propagation unless context is explicitly carried across the boundary
Sample intelligently: head sampling for cost, tail sampling to keep the errors
Log correlation ID and trace ID; span links for queue hops where there's no parent
questions.flow: traceparent at edge → propagate every hop → MDC into logs → carry context across async/queue
questions.trap: losing the trace at the first @Async or Kafka boundary

questions.text: 🏢 "One business transaction spans three microservices. How?
points: Not 2PC — you want Saga: local transaction per service + compensating action
Choreography (events, no coordinator, coupling hides in the topology) vs orchestration (explicit coordinator, visible state machine)
Outbox pattern for atomic DB-write + event-publish; CDC or a relay ships it
Consumers must be idempotent — delivery is at-least-once (01-PYTHON #24 is the same idea)
Accept eventual consistency explicitly and say what the user sees in between
questions.flow: local txn + compensations → orchestrate for visibility → outbox for atomicity → idempotent consumers
questions.trap: proposing distributed 2PC/XA, or ignoring the compensating path

questions.text: 🏢 "Service B is down and Service A keeps calling it. Stop the cascade.
points: Circuit breaker — open on failure-rate threshold, half-open probe, close on recovery
Aggressive timeouts first; without them the breaker never trips, threads just pile up
Bulkhead so B's failure can't consume A's whole pool (#33)
Retry only idempotent calls, bounded, with jitter — naive retry amplifies the outage
Define the fallback: cached value, degraded response, or fail fast — decide, don't default
questions.flow: timeout → breaker → bulkhead → jittered bounded retry → explicit fallback
questions.trap: retries without a breaker — you've built a self-inflicted DDoS

questions.text: We're a Java shop. Build us RAG on Spring.
points: Spring AI: VectorStore abstraction (pgvector, Redis, Qdrant…), EmbeddingModel, ChatClient
ETL-style ingestion: DocumentReader → TextSplitter → VectorStore.add — run it as a batch job, not in a request
QuestionAnswerAdvisor wires retrieval into the chat call; ChatClient fluent API composes it
Same architecture as Python: two pipelines, versioned contract (embed model + chunk scheme + index)
Java-specific wins: existing transactions, security, observability, and the ops story already exist
questions.flow: reader → splitter → embed → VectorStore ‖ query → advisor → ChatClient → cite
questions.trap: treating Spring AI as a different architecture — it's the same design, different bindings

questions.text: Expose our internal services to an LLM. How?
points: MCP — standard protocol for tools/resources/prompts; server exposes, client (the model host) consumes
Spring AI MCP server: annotate methods as tools, schema derived from types (same idea as 01-PYTHON #15)
Design tools coarse and intention-shaped, not one-per-endpoint — the model picks badly from 200 thin tools
Every tool call is untrusted input and a privileged action: authz per call, allowlists, human approval for destructive ops
Idempotency + timeouts per tool; the model will retry
questions.flow: expose intention-shaped tools → schema from types → authz per call → approve destructive → idempotent
questions.trap: auto-exposing your whole REST surface as tools

questions.text: It has to remember the conversation and stay in guardrails.
points: Advisors = interceptor chain for the chat call — memory, retrieval, logging, safety all compose here
ChatMemory implementations: in-memory for dev, JDBC/Redis for real; window or summary strategy
Memory is unbounded cost — cap turns, summarise older context, and say what you drop
Multi-tenant: memory keyed by conversation and tenant, or you leak across users
Guardrail advisors on both sides — input (injection, abuse) and output (PII, policy)
questions.flow: advisor chain → memory store keyed by tenant+conversation → window/summarise → guardrails both sides
questions.trap: unbounded chat memory — cost grows every turn and eventually blows the context window

questions.text: Tell me about the hardest production issue you've handled on the JVM.
points: Symptom in business terms — outage, latency, data issue — before any technical detail
Your first hypothesis and the evidence that killed it (this is the credibility beat)
The tool that actually found it: heap dump + MAT · GC log · JFR · thread dump
Fix, plus the guard you added so it can't recur silently — alert, test, assertion
The number: before → after
questions.flow: business symptom → wrong hypothesis → evidence → root cause → fix + guard → number
questions.trap: a tour of the debugging with no root cause named and no number
